# Book Pages 6–43 # Constituted Text Only;
Critical Apparatus Removed ## 1. Section. Primary Creation and Secondary Creation | Chapter 1 (P.1 I. 2. 84–119; P.2 V. 2. 83–117; Vi. I. 2. 10–66; cf. Ga. 4. 4–10)
He is the highest of the high, the supreme, the Supreme Self, the Grandfather;
devoid of form, color, and the like, He is free from all qualifying attributes. || 1 ||
Indeed, it shines forth as "the absolute" (kevala), being devoid of all qualities characterized by decrease, destruction, transformation, increase,
and birth. || 2 ||
He is considered peerless, dwelling equally everywhere,
manifesting in the form of Brahman.
It is studied thoroughly by the learned. || 3 ||
Devoid [of these], it can only be said that it exists eternally. || 2 ||
Since he dwells everywhere and everything dwells within him, he is therefore called Vāsudeva.
It is studied thoroughly by the learned. || 3 ||
That Brahman is supreme, eternal, unborn, undecaying, and immutable;
it is always of a single nature and stainless because of the absence of anything to be discarded. || 3 ||
All this, indeed, possesses the nature of both the manifest and the unmanifest.
Likewise, it exists in the form of the Person (puruṣa) and in the form of Time (kāla). || 4 ||
O twice-born one, the first form of the supreme Brahman is the Puruṣa;
likewise, the other two forms are the manifest (vyakta) and the unmanifest (avyakta), and time is yet another.

That which the wise perceive as the supreme, pure state of primordial matter (pradhāna), the individual soul (puruṣa), the manifest (vyakta), and time (kāla)—that indeed is the highest station of Viṣṇu. || 4 ||
Pradhāna, puruṣa, vyakta, and kāla, according to their respective divisions, are the causes for the existence of the forms [of the world] through maintenance, creation, and dissolution. || 4 ||
The manifest, as well as the unmanifest, the Puruṣa, and even Time—behold his activity, which is like that of a playing child! || 4 ||
That which is the unmanifest cause is called *pradhāna* by the best of seers;
it is the subtle primordial nature (*prakṛti*), eternal, and consisting of both the existent and the non-existent. || 45 ||
It is imperishable, without any other support, immeasurable, undecaying, and eternal;
it is devoid of sound and touch, and not composed of form and the other [sensory objects]. || 46 ||
That source of the world, consisting of the three qualities, is beginningless and is both the origin and the dissolution;
by it, everything was indeed pervaded after the dissolution and before [creation]. || 47 ||
The Brahmins who know the declarations of the Vedas, being self-restrained exponents of Brahman, recite this very same meaning which establishes the Pradhāna: || 48 ||
There was neither day nor night, neither sky nor earth; there was neither darkness nor light, nor anything else—
only the One, unperceivable by the intellect through the senses such as hearing.
At that time, the Puruṣa was the Brahman consisting of Pradhāna. || 49 ||
O Brahmin, those others— Prakṛti and Puruṣa— are indeed distinct from the essential nature of Viṣṇu;
they are held apart and separated by him through his other form.
O twice-born one, that which is by means of form is designated as "Time. || 410 ||

That which is manifest and established in primordial nature (prakṛti) during the great dissolution (pralaya), because it is withdrawn [into that state], is therefore called the "dissolution pertaining to primordial nature" (prākṛta-saṃhāra). || 411 ||
The Blessed Time is beginningless, O twice-born one, and its end is not known; from it, these continuous cycles of creation, maintenance, and dissolution proceed. || 412 ||
Then, O Maitreya, when that equilibrium of the qualities has subsided and the Puruṣa remains distinct, that form of Viṣṇu which is the very nature of Time prevails.
Then that supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self consisting of the universe, the all-pervading Lord of all beings, the Soul of all, the Supreme Lord; || 414 ||
When the time for creation arrived, Hari, according to his own will, entered both Pradhāna and Puruṣa— the perishable and the imperishable— and caused them to vibrate.
Just as a fragrance causes agitation by its mere presence, and not because it performs an active service upon the mind, so too is this Supreme Lord. || 416 ||
O Brahman, that very Puruṣottama is both the agitator and the object of agitation;
he abides even in the state of Pradhāna through contraction and expansion. || 417 ||
Having bowed to Him, who possesses the nature of both transformations and the subtle essence, as well as the form of Brahman and so forth,
I shall proclaim how He indeed brought about creation.
And likewise Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords, possesses a manifest nature. || 5 ||
But previously, O best of the twice-born, at the time of creation, the Lord of the world arose from his lotus-bed and brought forth the manifestations of the qualities and their characteristics.

The Great Principle (mahat) is threefold—consisting of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas—and it is enveloped by the principle of primordial matter (pradhāna), just as a seed is covered by its skin. || 7 ||
The Vaikārika, the Taijasa, and the Bhūtādi which is indeed Tāmasa—this threefold ego (ahaṃkāra) was born from the principle of Mahat. || 8 ||
Of the five elements and sense organs,
as well as together with the organs of action,
[there are] earth, water, and likewise fire.
And wind and space as well—
I shall describe each one according to its own nature, in successive order. || 9 ||
The waters, undergoing transformation, produced mere fragrance;
from that, the aggregate [earth] is born, and fragrance is considered its quality. || 15 ||
In each of those [gross elements], however, there is a "mere-that" (tanmātra); therefore, they are known as "mere-thats.
The tanmātras are non-specific (aviśeṣa), and for that reason, they are called non-specific. || 151 ||
They are neither peaceful nor terrible, nor are they deluded, being devoid of specific qualities;
this creation of the elements and subtle essences proceeds from the tamasic ego. || 152 ||
They say the sense organs are taijasa, while the ten deities are vaikārika; here, the eleventh, the mind, is also recorded as being a vaikārika deity.

The skin, the eye, the nose, the tongue, and the ear as the fifth—these five are indeed endowed with the faculty of discernment for the purpose of perceiving sound and the other sense objects. || 17 ||
The anus, the generative organ, the hands, the feet, and speech as the fifth are proclaimed; their functions are said to be excretion, procreation, manipulation, locomotion, and speaking. || 18 ||
Space, air, fire, water, and earth, O Brahmin, are joined with their respective qualities, beginning with sound, each succeeding one possessing more than the preceding. || 19 ||
Therefore, those specific states are remembered as being peaceful, terrible, and deluded. || 20 ||
Possessing diverse powers and existing separately, they were unable to create living beings without a collective union, as they had not come together in their entirety.
Having come together in mutual conjunction and being mutually dependent,
they attain complete unity, characterized as a single aggregate.
And because they are presided over by the Puruṣa and through the favor of the Unmanifest, those principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas produce the cosmic egg. || 23 ||

Gradually increased by that process, O one of great intelligence, an egg equal [in size] to a water bubble arose from the elements; that vast egg, resting upon the waters, is the primordial and supreme abode of Viṣṇu in his form as Brahmā. || 231 ||
There, that Lord of the World, Viṣṇu, who is by nature unmanifest yet possesses a manifest form, himself abides in the form of Brahmā. || 24 ||
Mount Meru became the amnion of that Great-Souled One, and the mountains were his chorion;
the oceans were the fetal waters of that most exalted being. || 25 ||
Within that egg was everything—the gods, asuras, and humans;
there were the continents and the oceans, along with the collection of worlds and the luminaries. || 26 ||

Then the egg is surrounded on the outside by water, fire, air, and ether, each ten times greater than the preceding; and the ego-principle (bhūtādi) is likewise surrounded by the Great Principle (mahat). || 27 ||
O Brahmin, the Great One (Mahat), together with all of them, is enveloped by the Unmanifest (Avyakta).

By all these coverings, and joined by all beings, the Egg is surrounded by these seven elemental coverings. || 28 || It is enclosed by the seven [sheaths] derived from primordial nature (prakṛti). || 28 ||
Just as the seed within a coconut fruit is surrounded by its outer husks,
so too Hari, the Lord of the Universe himself, dwells there while experiencing the quality of passion (rajas).
Having become Brahmā, he proceeds with the creation of this world. || 29 ||
And he protects the creation age after age as long as the differentiation of the kalpas lasts;
that one Lord Janārdana alone receives various designations. || 30 ||
The god who experiences the *sattva* quality is indeed possessed of virtues and possesses immeasurable prowess;
and at the end of the eon, he brings about the increase of *tamas*.
And he assumes a fierce form. || 31 ||
Janārdana has taken the form of Rudra. || 31 ||
O Maitreya, that most terrifying one devours all living beings;
and having devoured all beings when the world has been turned into a single ocean, [he remains].
That Supreme Lord reclines upon his serpent-couch;
and having awakened, he again effects creation, assuming the form of Brahmā. || 33 ||
Due to performing the acts of creation, preservation, and destruction, the one Lord Janārdana alone assumes the designations of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. || 34 ||
The Creator creates himself, and Viṣṇu protects that which is to be protected; at the end, he is withdrawn, for the Lord himself is the Destroyer. || 35 ||
Earth, water, fire, air, and space, as well as all the sense organs and the internal organ—that which is called the world is indeed the Puruṣa. || 36 ||

He alone is the Lord of all beings, the universal form, since he is imperishable; therefore, the creation and so forth, which reside within beings, are his very own and serve as his benefactors. || 37 ||
He alone is the object of creation and He is the creator; He alone protects, devours, and is protected.
Viṣṇu, whose form is the entirety [of all things] through the states beginning with Brahmā, is the most excellent, the giver of boons, and the one worthy of choice. || 38 ||
## Section One: Primary Creation and Secondary Creation | Chapter Two (Mr. 46.21–44; P.1 I.3.1–25a;
P.2 V.3.1–20a; Vi. I.3.1–25; cf. Kū. 5.1–23) Maitreya (Bhīṣma) said:
[Regarding] the one who is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) and immeasurable (*aprameya*)...
How can the agency of creation and so forth be possible even for a pure Great Soul,
O Brahmin? || 1 ||
Parāśara (Pulastya) said: The powers of all things lie beyond the scope of inconceivable knowledge.
Therefore, those powers of being, such as creation and the rest, belong to Brahman. || 1.1 ||
O best of those who radiate heat, understand that just as heat belongs to fire,
so it is in the case of creation.
The Blessed One proceeds. 1.2
The Lord known as Nārāyaṇa,
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
is said to have been born as the wise one.
It is indeed eternal, though [so called] by way of metaphorical designation. || 1.3 ||
Hiraṇyagarbha, the first of the gods,
is metaphorically called "beginningless," as he resides upon the pericarp of the earth-lotus.
Brahmā was born first. || 1 ||
The supreme lifespan of that great-souled one is indeed one hundred years,
according to the measurement of Brahmā himself.
Learn from me their number! || 2 ||
Ten *nimeṣas* are said to be one *kāṣṭhā*, and thirty *kāṣṭhās* are indeed one *kalā*.
Thirty of those *kalās* constitute a *muhūrta*. || 3 ||
A day and night is indeed recorded as consisting of thirty muhūrtas;
and thirty such days and nights [constitute a month].
Two fortnights are called a month. || 4 ||
By those six [months] there is one solstice; that constitutes a year, which is a day and night for the gods, and among them, the northern course is the day. || 5 ||
Know, O noble one, that the four yugas, designated as Kṛta, Tretā, and so forth, consist of twelve thousand divine years; now learn their specific divisions.
The Kṛta age is said to consist of four thousand years,
with four hundred years for each of its junctions (saṃdhyā).
And the twilight period is likewise of that same nature. || 7 ||
By his own measure, his lifespan is recorded as one hundred years;
that is called a *parārdha*, and half of that is [the other].
The term *parārdha* is thus designated. || 2 ||
O sinless one, understand from that which I have told you regarding the nature of time and of Viṣṇu how it relates to him.
The demonstration of measurement. || 2 ||
And likewise for other living beings,
both those that move and those that do not move—
such as the earth, mountains, oceans, and so forth.
And of all beings without exception, O best of men! || 2 ||
O best of sages, fifteen *nimeṣas* are said to be one *kāṣṭhā*;
thirty *kāṣṭhās* are one *kalā*, and thirty [kalās are one *muhūrta*].
The ritual concerning the divisions of time (kalās) and the moments (muhūrtas). || 3 ||
A human day and night is said to consist of that same number of muhūrtas;
there are that many days and nights [in a month].
A month consists of two fortnights. || 4 ||
There are two solstices, southern and northern:
the southern solstice is the night of the gods, and the northern is their day. || 5 ||
The four yugas, known as Kṛta, Tretā, and so forth, consist of twelve thousand divine years; learn their division from me! (6)
Four, three, two,
and one thousand divine years, respectively, for the Kṛta and the other ages.
Those who know the past have said this regarding the ages. || 7 ||
The Tretā age consists of three thousand divine years and three hundred;
its dawn and its twilight are equal to that [total].
And the twilight period (saṃdhyāṃśa) is likewise of that same nature. || 8 ||
The Dvāpara age consists of two thousand years and two hundred;
its twilight period is likewise declared to be the same.
Two hundred years is its constituent part. || 9 ||
O best of the twice-born, Kali lasts for one thousand divine years,
as do its dawn and twilight periods.
The two hundred [verses] have been extracted. || 91 ||
This period of twelve thousand years, called a *yuga*, has been established by the poets;
this multiplied by a thousand [is a *kalpa*].
Oh, how sublime is this utterance! || 10 ||
The preceding twilight (pūrvasaṃdhyā) there is said to consist of hundreds of those same measures,
and the portion of twilight (saṃdhyāṃśaka) is equal to that.
For he is indeed the one immediately following the Yuga. || 8 ||
O best of sages, that period of time which lies between the twilight (saṃdhyā) and the twilight-fraction (saṃdhyāṃśa) is to be known as the name of a Yuga.
It is designated by the names Kṛta, Tretā, and so forth. || 9 ||
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali— these constitute the four yugas;
you have declared that [cycle] to be a thousandfold.
O Sage, this is a day of Brahmā. || 10 ||
O Brahman, fourteen Manus arise during a single day of Brahmā; hear now their duration as determined by time. || 11 ||
The seven sages, the gods, Śakra, Manu, and his sons, the kings, are indeed created at one and the same time, and are withdrawn in the same manner as before. || 12 ||
O best of beings, a period of seventy-one cycles of four yugas, plus a little more, constitutes the duration of a Manvantara, the time of a Manu and of the suns and other luminaries. (13)
Eight hundred thousand according to divine reckoning, and additionally fifty-two thousand more. || 14 ||
But thirty full crores were counted by number, O twice-born one.
And likewise, sixty-seven million others, O Great Sage. || 15 ||
And twenty thousand years—this is the count of a *manvantara* according to human years here on earth, excluding the additional period. (16)
For this period of fourteen-fold duration is remembered as a day of Brahmā;
at its conclusion, O Brahmin, a dissolution is proclaimed by the wise as the "occasional" (naimittika) one.
The world of the earth (bhūrloka), the world of the atmosphere (bhuvarloka), and the celestial world (svarloka) are all subject to destruction. || 17 ||
In the same way, Maharloka perishes,
and its inhabitants also depart due to the heat.
They indeed go to Janaloka. || 18 ||
When the three worlds have become a single ocean, Brahmā indeed sleeps during the night;
that night is of exactly the same duration as that day.
At the end of that, it is created again. || 19 ||
In this manner, a Brāhmaṇa lives for one year, and in that same manner for a hundred years;
for the maximum lifespan of that great-souled one is indeed one hundred such years. || 20 ||
Fifty such years are proclaimed to be a *parārdha*.
O sinless Brāhmaṇa, one *parārdha* of his has already passed.
At its conclusion, there occurred a great kalpa widely renowned as Pāṇḍika. || 21 ||
O twice-born one, this first Kalpa of the present second Parārdha is designated as Vārāha. || 22 ||

**Section One: Primary Creation and Secondary Creation | Chapter Three** (Krauṣṭuki said: "How indeed did Brahmā create? (Varuṇa replied: "In the beginning, O sage, the Self-born Lord, having meditated for a long time, created from his mind the seven great-souled mental sons (mānasaputra) who were equal to himself. They were Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and the seventh, Vasiṣṭha. These seven great-souled ones are known as the creators of all worlds. From these seven, O Brahmin, the entire world was produced. From them, the seven Manus, the deities, and the great ṛṣis were born. From them, the world consisting of mobile and immobile beings was produced. Furthermore, from his forehead, he created Rudra, who was half-female and half-male. He created him for the sake of destroying the triple-world. Then, O Brahmin, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) created the waters, the sky, the earth, the wind, the clouds, the stars, the rivers, and the oceans. Having thus created the world with its mobile and immobile beings, he established the eternal order of the world. He assigned the gods to heaven, the Pitṛs to the intermediate space, and humans and animals to the earth. He established the sun and moon in the sky for the purpose of illuminating the world. He assigned the seasons, the months, the fortnights, and the years. He established the divisions of time, such as the kṣaṇas, lavas, muhūrtas, days, nights, and years. He established the four ages: Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali. He assigned duties to the various castes and stages of life according to their respective natures. He ordained the Vedas, the sacrifices, the mantras, and the rituals. He established the distinctions between the righteous and the unrighteous, and the paths of happiness and suffering. Thus, O best of Brahmins, the Self-born Lord created this entire universe through his power of yoga.
Krauṣṭuki said:

"How indeed did Brahmā create? (Varuṇa continued: "Having first created the mental sons, the Self-born Lord then created the Prajāpatis from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet. From his mouth he created the Brāhmaṇas, from his arms the Kṣatriyas, from his thighs the Vaiśyas, and from his feet the Śūdras. From his eyes he created the Sun, from his ears the Wind, from his mind the Moon, and from his speech the Vedas. From his navel he created the ether, from his chest the air, from his belly the earth, and from his head the sky. From his hair he created the plants and herbs, and from his sweat the small creatures. From his tears he created the clouds, and from his blood the oceans. Thus, O Brahmin, the Grandfather created the world with its manifold forms. Krauṣṭuki said: "How indeed did Brahmā create? (Varuṇa continued: "When the world had become one vast expanse of water, the Self-born Lord, desiring to produce diverse creatures, first created the great elements. From the union of the elements, he created the subtle bodies (liṅga-dehas). Then, by means of the power of time, he brought forth the gross bodies. He created the mountains, the forests, the rivers, and the oceans. He created the celestial bodies, the planets, and the constellations. He established the laws of karma and the fruits of actions. Thus, O sage, the Self-born Lord, through his supreme intelligence, brought forth this entire universe. Krauṣṭuki said: "How indeed did Brahmā create? (Varuṇa continued: "The Self-born Lord, having first created the mental sons, then created the Prajāpatis. From them, the Manus, the deities, and the great ṛṣis were born. From them, the world was produced. He created the four classes of beings: the viviparous, the oviparous, those born from moisture, and those born from sprouts. He assigned specific duties to each class according to their inherent nature. He ordained the performance of sacrifices, the study of the Vedas, and the practice of austerities. He established the distinction between the righteous
The Blessed One is the first creator of beings, the Lord of creatures, the divine Master;
tell me that in detail! || 1 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Brahmin, I shall tell you how the Blessed One created [the world].
The eternal creator of the world [is the one who made] the entire universe, both stationary and moving. || 2 ||
At the end of the lotus, at the time of dissolution,
the Lord Brahmā, having awakened from his sleep during the night and being filled with the quality of goodness (sattva), beheld the world as empty. || 3 ||
Nārāyaṇa is supreme and inconceivable; he is the Lord even of those who are supreme, the Blessed One whose nature is Brahman.
[It is] beginningless and the source of all things. || 3 ||
And in this regard, they cite this verse concerning Nārāyaṇa, the god who is the very nature of Brahman and the source and dissolution of the world: || 4 ||
"We have heard that 'waters' (āpaḥ) are indeed 'nārāḥ' because they are the bodies (tanavaḥ);
he (Puruṣa) lies within them."
Therefore, he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa. || 5 ||
Maitreya said:
Just as at the beginning of the kalpa, that Blessed One known as Nārāyaṇa was Brahmā.
He created all beings;
tell that, O great sage! || 1 ||
Parāśara (Pulastya) said: The Lord Brahmā, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa, created all living beings.
Just as the divine Lord of Prajāpati [is the source], listen to that from me! || 2 ||
At the conclusion of the past kalpa, the Lord, having arisen from his night’s sleep,
declared: "The waters are called *nārāḥ*."
The waters are indeed the sons of Nara;
they were his first abode (ayana), and for that reason he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa. || 5 ||
Having awakened in that water, Prajāpati perceived the earth submerged within it; through inference, he desired to effect its extraction. || 6 ||
Just as in former ages at the beginnings of the kalpas he assumed other bodies such as those of the fish and the tortoise, so too did he take on the form of a boar.
Having assumed a form composed of the Vedas and sacrifices for the sake of the stability of the entire world,
he who is all-pervading and the source of all entered into the waters. || 8 ||
Having lifted it up from Pātāla, he released the earth into the waters,
while remaining in Janaloka with the Siddhas.
The Lord of the World was being meditated upon.
|| 9 || Then, seeing him who had arrived at the surface of Pātāla, the Goddess Earth, bowing down and humbled by devotion, offered praise. || 10 ||
The Earth said:
Salutations to you, the soul of all beings; salutations to you, the Supreme Self!
Lift me up from this today; it was from you that I arose in the beginning. || 11 ||
I was previously extracted from you; I am composed of you, O Janārdana, as are all other beings without exception, beginning with the ether. || 11.1 ||

Salutations be unto you, O Supreme Self; salutations be unto you, O Soul of the Person. Salutations to you who take the form of both the unmanifest and the manifest Pradhāna, and who are Time itself! || 12 ||

You are the creator of all beings, you are their protector, and you are the bringer of their destruction; O Lord, in the acts of creation and the rest, you assume the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra!
He made Sanandana and the other sages, who were already free from stain, once again the very abode of purity;
their breaths moved everywhere around them. || 22 ||

As that Great Boar, whose flanks are wet with water, rises up after tearing open the earth and shakes his body consisting of the Vedas, the sages dwelling within the expanse of space rejoice. || 23 ||
Those yogis who dwell among the people of the world, Sanandana and the others, their hearts overcome with joy, praised him while bowing their necks in prostration.
The supporter of the earth, with eyes steady and haughty. || 23 ||
Victory to Keśava, the Supreme Lord of lords, O Master who wields the mace, conch, sword, and discus;
You are the Lord who is the cause of the creation, destruction, and maintenance [of the world].
You alone are that; there is no other supreme state. || 24 ||

O Lord, the Vedas are in Your feet, the sacrificial posts are Your tusks, the sacrifices and the altars are in Your teeth, fire is Your tongue, and the darbha grasses are Your body hairs; You alone are the Person of Sacrifice! || 25 ||
O Great-souled One, night and day are your two eyes;
the state of Brahman, the refuge of all, is your head; and the entire collection of hymns is the mass of your matted hair.
O God, the nose [is] all the sacrificial oblations! || 25 ||
O Lord, you are the sacrificial ladle, the deep resonance of the Sāman chants,
and the entire assembly of priests within the eastern hall;
you are the merit of public works and sacrifices, and the scripture of Dharma itself.
O Blessed One, eternal Self, be gracious! || 25 ||
O you whose form is the universe, we know you as the one who has traversed the earth with the steps of the Vedas, the primordial foundation, and the imperishable;
you are the Supreme Lord of the universe.
Be gracious, for you are the Lord of all that moves and is stationary! || 25 ||
O Lord, as you wade through the lotus grove, this entire circle of the earth appears to be resting upon the tips of your fangs.
Like a lotus leaf bearing mud. || 25 ||
O Lord of incomparable power, just as the space between heaven and earth is pervaded by Your body, so too is this entire world pervaded; for the welfare of the universe, please become manifest.
You alone are the Supreme Self; there is no other, O Lord of the world!
This greatness belongs to you, by which this entire universe of moving and non-moving beings is pervaded. || 27 ||
This which is seen as having form is yours, whose nature is knowledge;
those who are not yogis perceive it as the form of the world through deluded cognition. || 27 ||
Those lacking wisdom, perceiving this entire world—which is in its true nature pure consciousness—as being of the nature of material objects, wander in the deluge of ignorance. || 28 ||
But those whose minds are pure and who possess the knowledge of wisdom, O Supreme Lord, perceive the entire world as consisting of knowledge and as Your very form. || 29 ||
Be gracious, O Soul of all beings! For the welfare of the world, O immeasurable one, O lotus-eyed one, lift up this earth that is submerged! (30)
"O Blessed One, Govinda, you are overflowing with the quality of goodness (sattva); O Lord, lift up this earth and bring about the welfare of the entire world! || 31 ||
May this engagement in creation of yours be for the benefit of the worlds;
let it be so. Homage be to you! Grant us well-being, O lotus-eyed one! (31)
Thus being praised, the Supreme Self, the Supporter of the Earth, [spoke].
He swiftly lifted up the earth and placed it back in the great ocean. || 32 ||
Upon that flood of water, he stands like a great ship; and because his body is so vast, the earth does not sink under him. || 33 ||
Then, having leveled the earth, the Lord, the beginningless Puruṣottama, constructed mountains upon the ground according to their respective divisions.
When the previous creation was being consumed by the Samvartaka fire,
[he saw] all those who had been burnt in the previous creation.
By the power of Amogha, he whose desires are unfailing created mountains upon the surface of the earth. || 35 ||
By that fire, those mountains were shattered on all sides upon the earth. || 35 ||
The mountains were submerged in the single vast ocean, and the waters were condensed by the wind wherever they had settled.
In each of those places, they became immovable. || 35 ||
Then, having divided the earth into its seven continents exactly as they are, he fashioned the four worlds beginning with Bhūr, just as before. || 36 ||
This very thing was previously shown to Brahmā by Viṣṇu,
the God of gods, who was pleased.
You are the God, the Supreme Person. || 37 ||
This world must be supported and protected with effort by both you and me;
[as for] those who are the leaders of the asuras—
The boon has now been granted by me. || 38 ||
O Lord, for the sake of the welfare of the gods, you must slay him!
I shall perform the creation.
"And she must be protected by you, O Lord.
Having been addressed thus, the all-pervading Viṣṇu departed;
the Lord then created the gods and the rest. || 39 ||
Then that god, assuming the form of Brahmā and enveloped by rajas,
the Blessed One, performed the act of creation.
Hari bears four faces. || 37 ||
He was merely the instrumental cause in the act of creation of those things to be created,
having become the primary causal agent.
For from that indeed [proceed] the powers of creation. || 38 ||
"Nothing else whatsoever is perceived except for the single sign;
it is led [there], O best of those who radiate heat."
By its own power, it brings the thing to the state of being a real entity. || 39 ||
## Section One: Primary Creation and Secondary Creation | Chapter Four [Maitreya said:
"How did that Lord create the gods, the celestial sages, the ancestors, and the Dānavas?"
Humans, animals, trees, and so forth, whose abodes are the earth, the sky, and the water; || 11 ||
O twice-born one, tell me in truth what qualities, what essential nature, and what inherent character the world possessed when Brahmā created it at the beginning of the creation! || 12 ||
Parāśara said:
O Maitreya, listen with a well-composed mind; I shall tell you how that Lord, the Sovereign, created all beings, beginning with the gods.
As he was contemplating creation as in former ages at the beginning of the kalpas,
a creation consisting of darkness appeared, not preceded by conscious intent.
Darkness, delusion, great delusion, gloom, and that which is called utter darkness—this fivefold ignorance manifested from the Great Soul. || 2 ||
The creation, existing in fivefold states, belongs to one who meditates yet lacks awakening;
it is enveloped by darkness and covered like a jar of seeds.
Without light both outside and inside, they are indeed motionless and devoid of consciousness. || 3 ||
Lacking light both outside and within, its nature concealed, it is of the character of a mountain. || 3 ||
Since the primary Nāgas were spoken of, this [creation] is therefore called the primary creation (mukhya-sarga).
Having seen that creation to be ineffective, he then reflected upon another. || 4 ||
As he was bursting forth with creation, the Tiryaksrotas (the downward-streaming) turned outwards;
because it proceeded obliquely, it is therefore known as Tiryaksrotas. || 5 ||
These are known as beasts and the like; they are dominated by darkness (tamas), devoid of knowledge, followers of wrong paths, and those who imagine themselves wise while remaining ignorant. (6)
Those consisting of egoism and self-conceit are of twenty-eight kinds;
they are all internally luminous, yet mutually veiled.
Considering that [state] also to be ineffective, another arose for him as he meditated;
the third, however, was the "upward-streaming" (ūrdhvasrotas), which proceeded upward with a predominance of sattva. || 8 ||
Abounding in happiness and joy, they are unobstructed both internally and externally;
luminous within and without, they are known as those whose stream of existence flows upward. || 9 ||
But for him whose soul was satisfied, that third creation is remembered as the divine (deva-sarga); when that creation was completed, there then arose joy in Brahmā. || 10 ||
Then, having recognized those [previous beings] as unsuccessful, he reflected upon another, superior creation of successful beings, arising from the primary creation and the rest. || 11 ||
As he was thus meditating, being one whose meditation was fixed on truth, there then emerged from the Unmanifest the Arvāk-srotas, the achiever. || 12 ||
Because they proceed toward what is below, they are therefore called "downward-streaming" (arvāksrotas).
They are characterized by an abundance of light, yet are dominated by darkness, with passion being predominant. || 13 ||
Therefore, those who repeatedly perform [actions] experience much suffering;
such humans are manifest both outwardly and inwardly, and they are practitioners. || 14 ||
The fifth is the creation of favor (anugraha-sarga), and it is established as fourfold:
through error (viparyaya), through attainment (siddhi), through power (śakti), and likewise through contentment (tuṣṭi). || 15 ||
Furthermore, they indeed know the past and the present objects of those beings beginning with the Bhūtas; that is called the sixth creation. || 16 ||

All those who possess grasping are likewise devoted to sharing; they should be known as the "impellers" (codanā), and those beginning with the elements (bhūtādi) are characterized by a lack of moral discipline (aśīla). || 17 ||
Thus, O best of sages, these six creations have been described here;
the first is to be known as the creation of Mahat, which belongs to Brahmā. || 18 ||
The second, however, is the creation of the subtle elements (tanmātra), which is indeed remembered as the elemental creation (bhūtasarga).
The third is the creation of the Vaikārika [intellect], which is remembered as the creation of the senses (aindriyaka). || 19 ||
Thus this primary creation (prākṛta-sarga) has arisen, not preceded by conscious intent.
But the fourth is the primary creation of beings (mukhya-sarga); indeed, the immobile entities are known as the primary beings.
That which is called the horizontal stream (tiryak-srotas) is the fifth, the animal creation (tairyagyonya).
Likewise, the sixth is that of the upward-streaming ones (ūrdhva-srotas), which is known as the divine creation (deva-sarga). || 21 ||
Then follows the seventh creation, that of the downward-streaming beings, which is human;
the eighth is the creation of grace, consisting of both the qualities of goodness (sattva) and darkness (tamas). || 22 ||

These five are known as the modified (vaikṛta) creations; the three primordial (prākṛta) ones are traditionally recorded. The ninth is remembered as the Kaumāra creation, which is both primordial and modified. || 23 ||
Thus, these nine creations of Prajāpati have indeed been fully described;
they are both primary (prākṛta) and secondary (vaikṛta), and are the fundamental causes of the world. What else do you wish to hear concerning the Lord of the World as he creates? || 24 ||
## Section One: Primary Creation and Secondary Creation | Chapter Five (Kauṣītaki said: "The primary creation has been described in brief."
It has been correctly explained by the Blessed One to me; O Brahmin, please tell me in detail about the existence of the gods and others. || 1 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Brahmin, [the world] is conditioned by previous actions, both auspicious and inauspicious.
For as long as they are not liberated from that manifestation, they are indeed withdrawn during the dissolution.
The fourfold classes of beings, from the gods down to the immovable, were born as mental creations from Brahmā while he was performing the work of creation. || 3 ||
Then, desiring to create the fourfold group—gods, asuras, ancestors, and humans—he joined his own self to these waters. || 4 ||
When the self of Prajāpati was composed of yoga, the quality of darkness (tamas) became predominant;
then, from the thighs of him desiring to create, the Asuras were first born. || 5 ||
Then he cast off that body whose nature consists of the quality of darkness (*tamas*).
Maitreya (Bhīṣma) said:
"The creation has been described in brief."
O Sage, O most excellent of sages, I wish to hear from you in detail concerning the gods and others. || 1 ||
Parāśara (Pulastya) said:
"Those [beings] are indeed conditioned by their previous actions, both wholesome and unwholesome."
O Brahmin, the fourfold classes of beings, beginning with the gods and ending with the stationary,
were cast off by him as a worn-out body.
Immediately, night was born. || 6 ||
Desiring to emit another body, he attained joy; then, due to the abundance of *sattva*, the gods [arose].
They were born from his mouth. || 7 ||
And that all-pervading Lord of Beings cast off even that body;
and it, having been discarded, [remained] for a day.
It was born consisting mostly of living beings. || 8 ||
Then he assumed another body consisting solely of the quality of sattva;
as he regarded it as his father, his ancestors were born from it. || 9 ||
Having created the ancestors, that Lord then emitted her as well;
once emitted, she became the twilight (saṃdhyā), situated between day and night.
Then that Lord assumed another body consisting of the quality of rajas;
from that, human beings were born.
Arising from mere particles of passion. || 11 ||
Having created human beings, that Lord then cast off his body,
and from it the moonlight was produced.
And that which occurs at the end of night and at the beginning of day. || 12 ||
But that body, once abandoned by him, O Maitreya, became the night. || 6 ||
Desiring to create while residing in another body,
he attained joy; thereupon, the gods emerged, overflowing with the quality of purity (sattva).
From the mouth of Brahmā, O twice-born one. || 7 ||
Having abandoned that body as well,
the day became filled with living beings;
for they were stronger at night.
The Asuras [rule] at night; the deities, by day. || 8 ||
Then he assumed another body consisting solely of the quality of sattva; from that,
[another] was born, in whom the quality of rajas was predominant.
O best of the twice-born, [this applies to] human beings. || 11 ||
The Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) also quickly abandoned that body immediately;
it then became the moonlight.
That which is designated as "prior" is called *saṃdhyā*. || 12 ||
Thus, O twice-born one, these are the bodies of that wise God of gods: they are known as night, day, twilight, and moonlight.

Moonlight, twilight, and likewise day—these three consist of the quality of goodness (sattva); night consists of the quality of darkness (tamas). Therefore, it indeed has three watches (triyāmikā). || 122 ||
Therefore, the gods [prevail] by day, while the Asuras, accompanied by their forces, do so at night; the humans prevail when the moonlight appears, and likewise the ancestors during the twilight.
They become powerful and invincible against their adversaries; of this there is no doubt.
Having encountered the opposite of that, however—
And they undergo reversal. || 13 ||
Moonlight, night, day, and twilight—these four, O Lord, are indeed the bodies of Brahmā, which are based upon the three qualities (guṇas). || 14 ||
Then, having produced these four,
Prajāpati created another body composed of rajas and tamas during the night.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, he seized it. || 15 ||
In that darkness, the unborn Lord created beings emaciated by hunger, deformed and bearded, in order to devour [the world].
And they began to consume that body. || 16 ||
Those others who said, "Let us protect them," were the Rākṣasas; and those who said, "Let us devour them," [were the Piśācas].
O twice-born one, they are called *yakṣas* because of their devouring (*yakṣaṇāt*). || 17 ||
Seeing them, the hair of that wise woman fell out in grief, as did her teeth,
which were missing from the upper row.
But those [teeth] of Brahmā were from his head. || 18 ||
Because they glide (sarpaṇa), they became serpents (sarpas); because they are devoid [of feet] (hīna), they are known as "without-feet" (ahayas).
Then, out of anger upon seeing the serpents, he created beings of wrathful nature from his own rage. || 19 ||
From his dark-brown urine were born fierce flesh-eating spirits;
from his dung, the Gandharvas were born as his sons. || 20 ||
Drinking [the essence], they brought forth speech; therefore, they are remembered as Gandharvas.
When these eight divine wombs had been created, that Lord [proceeded further]. || 21 ||
Then, by his own will, he created other birds from his own body.
Those who said to him, "Protect us! became the Rākṣasas because of that.
Others said, "Let us eat," and those who did so became the Yakṣas because of their eating (jakṣaṇāt). || 17 ||
Then, seeing those [creatures] who were unpleasant to him,
the hair of the Creator fell away; and once fallen from his head, it grew back again.
They ascended that head. || 18 ||
Then the Creator of the World, becoming enraged, brought forth from his own self a being composed of anger. || 19 ||
As he was milking the cow, Gandharvas emerged from her at that very moment.
Having created these, the Lord Brahmā was impelled by their respective powers.
Then he created goats from his mouth, and from his chest he created rams. || 22 ||
From his belly he created cows, and from his two sides he brought forth Brahmā;
and from his feet he produced horses, elephants, donkeys, gayals, and deer.
From his body hair were born camels, mules, antelopes, and other species, as well as plants bearing fruits and roots. || 24 ||
Therefore, at the beginning of the eon, at the onset of the Tretā Yuga,
having thus created the animals and the medicinal herbs, he then—
And the all-pervading Lord performed a sacrifice in that ritual. || 25 ||
The cow, the goat, the man, the sheep, the horse, the mule, and the donkey—these they call domestic animals; now learn from me those that are wild. || 26 ||
Beasts of prey, cloven-hoofed animals, elephants, monkeys with birds as the fifth, aquatic animals as the sixth, and reptiles as the seventh—these are the classes of animals. || 27 ||
From his first mouth, he fashioned the Gāyatrī, the Ṛg-veda verses, the Trivṛt-stoma, the Rathantara-sāman, and the Agniṣṭoma among sacrifices. || 28 ||
From his southern mouth, he emitted the Yajus formulas, the Triṣṭubh metre, the fifteenfold Stoma, the Bṛhat Sāman, and likewise the Uktha. || 29 ||
From his western mouth, he created the Sāman chants, the Jagatī meter, the seventeen-fold Stoma, the Vairūpa, and the Atirātra sacrifice. || 30 ||
Then from his northern mouth, he created the Ekaviṃśa, the Atharvāṇa, the Āptoryāmaṇa, the Anuṣṭubh, and the Svarāj. || 31 ||
At the beginning of the kalpa, the powerful and all-pervading Lord created lightning, thunderbolts, clouds, red-colored portents, rainbows, and birds.
High and low beings were born from his limbs;
having first created the fourfold [order], and having created the gods, asuras, and ancestors, Prajāpati created human beings as well. || 32 ||
Then he created living beings; thereafter, at the beginning, he again created both the immobile and the mobile. He was the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) of the Kalpa:
[he created] the Yakṣas, Piśācas, Gandharvas, and likewise the hosts of Apsarases. || 33 ||
Nagas, kinnaras, and rakshasas; birds, cattle, wild animals, and serpents; that which is imperishable and that which is perishable—indeed, all this that is both stationary and moving. || 34 ||
Then the Lord Brahmā, the original creator and all-pervading one, emitted them; whatever actions they had performed in a previous creation, those he assigned to them once again. || 35 ||
As they are created again and again, they enter into those very same [dispositions]:
violence and non-violence, gentleness and cruelty, righteousness and unrighteousness, truth and falsehood.
Pervaded by that, they attain it; therefore, that is what pleases him.
He is the Lord over the objects of the senses, the elements, and the bodies. || 37 ||
The Creator himself has emitted diversity and the application [of things], as well as the names and forms of beings and the expansion of their activities. || 38 ||
From the words of the Vedas alone, he created the gods and others at the beginning,
as well as the names of the seers and those creations that exist among the gods. || 39 ||
At the end of the night, he bestows [the fruits] upon those born and others as well,
just as the various seasonal signs appear in their turn according to the seasons.
Those very same kinds of beings appear in such a manner at the beginnings of the ages;
such are the creations of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest.
At the end of the night, for one who has awakened, these indeed come to pass in every kalpa. || 41 ||
**Section One: Primary Creation and Secondary Creation | Chapter Six** Maitreya (Bhīṣma) said:
"You have described the downward-flowing stream (*arvāksrotas*), which is that of human beings."
O Brahman, speak in detail how Brahmā created him. || 1 ||
O great sage, tell us how he created the castes and their qualities, and what the traditional duties of those beginning with the Brahmins are said to be. || 2 ||

Parāśara (Pulastya) said: O best of the twice-born, as Brahmā was meditating upon *sattva* and desiring to create the world, beings characterized by an abundance of *sattva* were born from his mouth. || 3 ||
From his chest, others arose from an abundance of *rajas*, and from his thighs, others arose from an abundance of both *rajas* and *tamas*. || 4 ||
O best of the twice-born, Brahmā created other beings from his feet; they were all dominated by *tamas*, and from them arose this fourfold social order (*cāturvarṇya*). || 5 ||
O best of the twice-born, the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras emerged from his feet,
thighs, chest, and mouth respectively.
For the accomplishment of the sacrifice, O highly fortunate one, Brahmā indeed created all this— the fourfold order of society, which is the supreme means for performing the sacrifice.
O knower of dharma, the gods are nourished by sacrifices, and human beings are nourished by the release of rain; thus sacrifices, which are the cause of well-being, bring nourishment to all. || 8 ||
These are always brought forth by those men who are ever devoted to their own duty, who are free from contrary conduct, who are virtuous, and who walk upon the path of the righteous. || 9 ||
Then, that which is called the abode of Vairiñca, consisting of time itself,
[is characterized by] an extreme falling into saṃsāra.
Terrible, yet possessing very little essence. || 14 ||
For there were indeed priyaṅgu grains, noble koradūṣa grains, and cīnaka grains. || 21 ||
Māṣas, mudgas, masūras, niṣpāvas, along with kulatthas, āḍhakīs, caṇakas, and śaṇas—these are recorded as the seventeen [types of legumes]. || 22 ||
"Thus, O Sage, these are the species of cultivated plants;
there are fourteen types of medicinal herbs, both sacrificial and belonging to the domestic and wild varieties. (23)
Rice, barley, beans, wheat, millet, sesame, and priyaṅgu as the seventh—these are indeed [the grains]; but kulattha is the eighth. || 24 ||
Then there are śyāmāka, nīvāra, jartila together with gavedhuka, as well as bamboo-seeds (veṇuyava) and likewise markaṭaka, O Sage;
these fourteen are indeed recorded as the cultivated and wild medicinal herbs.
For the accomplishment of sacrifice; sacrifice is likewise their supreme cause. || 26 ||
And these, together with sacrifice, are the supreme cause of living beings;
therefore, the wise who know the higher and the lower perform sacrifices. || 27 ||
O best of sages, the daily performance of sacrifices brings benefit to men; when performed, it bestows peace. (28)
But those in whose minds, O Great-minded One, that drop of evil produced by Time increased, they did not set their minds upon sacrifices. || 28.1 ||
Likewise, the doctrines of the Vedas, the Vedas themselves, and whatever pertains to sacrificial rites and the like—
They all censured him, those who were obstructing the sacrifice.
They became destroyers of the path of worldly activity, revilers of the Vedas, evil-minded, of wicked conduct, and crooked in their intentions. || 28.3 ||
Once the means of livelihood were fully established, Prajāpati, having created living beings,
fixed the boundaries according to their respective places and qualities.

O best among the upholders of dharma, [you have described] the duties of the social classes and the stages of life, as well as the worlds of those belonging to all classes who correctly observe their duties. || 30 ||
The station of Prajāpati is ordained for Brāhmaṇas who perform their duties;
the station of Indra is for Kṣatriyas who do not retreat in battles. || 31 ||
The station of the Maruts is for Vaiśyas who follow their own duty;
the station of the Gandharvas is for those born of the Śūdra caste who follow the practice of service. || 32 ||
That same station which is ordained for the eighty-eight thousand ascetics who have drawn up their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas) is also for those who dwell with their teacher. || 33 ||
The station of the Seven Sages is indeed remembered as belonging to the forest-dwellers;
that of Prajāpati belongs to householders, and that known as Brahman belongs to renunciants. || 34 ||
The immortal abode of yogis is that which is the supreme station of Viṣṇu;
for those who are single-mindedly devoted, ever-exerting, meditative, and indeed yogis— || 35 ||
That is their supreme state, which the wise behold.
The moon, the sun, and the other planets go forth and return again. || 36 ||

Even now they do not turn back; even now those who have Nārāyaṇa as their supreme goal do not turn back. Contemplating the twelve-syllable mantra, [they avoid] Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, and Raurava. (37)
The terrible Asipatravana, Kālasūtra, and Avīci—
these are declared to be the abodes for those who revile the Veda, those who obstruct sacrifices, and those who abandon their own dharma. (38)
**Chapter 7: Section 1.
Primary Creation and Secondary Creation** Then, as he was meditating, mental offspring were born to him, together with those effects and causes produced from his own body. || 1 ||
The knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas) emerged from the limbs of that wise one;
all those who were previously mentioned by me came forth. || 2 ||
From the gods down to the stationary beings, all remain within the domain of the three qualities (guṇas).
Thus were the beings created, both the stationary and the moving. || 3 ||
When all those offspring of that wise man did not increase in number,
he then created other mental sons who were like himself.
Bhṛgu, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, as well as Aṅgiras, Marīci, Dakṣa, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha, who was likewise born of his mind. || 5 ||
"These are the nine Brahmās," such is the certainty established in the Purāṇas.
Then Brahmā again created Rudra, who was born from his own wrath, as well as Saṃkalpa and Dharma, the progenitor even of the former ones. || 6 ||
And those such as Sanandana and others who were previously created by the Creator did not become attached to the worlds, for they were indifferent toward living beings.
For all those great-souled ones had attained knowledge, were free from passion, and devoid of envy; thus they remained indifferent toward the creation of the world.

A great wrath arose in Brahmā, capable of consuming the three worlds. From that wrath of his, there emerged a light, blazing with garlands of flames, which then began to burn the entire triple world. || 9 ||
Then, from his forehead, which was furrowed by a frown and inflamed with anger, Rudra emerged, possessing a radiance like that of the midday sun. || 10 ||
Then Brahmā, having said to that Pracaṇḍa—who possessed a body both half-female and half-male and who was exceedingly large-bodied—"Divide yourself"—vanished from that place. || 11 ||
Thus addressed, he divided himself into two forms— femininity and masculinity— and he further split that masculinity into ten parts and one part.
With both gentle and ungentle forms, and likewise with peaceful ones, that Lord, the God, divided womanhood into many parts through his own forms, both dark and light. || 13 ||
Then, O twice-born one, he made himself alone— Manu, the self-existent Lord born of Brahmā— the first protector of creatures.
And the powerful Svāyambhuva Manu, the god, took that woman Śatarūpā—whose impurities had been cleansed by asceticism—as his wife. (15)
And from that Puruṣa was born the goddess Śatarūpā, who gave birth to Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, both renowned for their own deeds. || 16 ||
Two daughters, as well as Ṛddhi and Prasūti. Then the father gave Prasūti to Dakṣa.
Likewise, he formerly bestowed supernatural power upon Ruci. || 17 ||
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda were born [to her], known by the names Prasūti and Ākūti. || 16 ||
And he gave two daughters, Prasūti and Dakṣā, who were knowers of dharma and endowed with beauty, nobility, and virtue.
[He established] the intention for the sake of radiance in the past. || 17 ||
Prajāpati took hold of it; from that, Dakṣiṇa was born.
From that couple arose a pair of children: Yajña as the son and Mahāhāvī as the daughter. || 18 ||
From the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of the sacrifice, twelve sons were born;
they are known as the Yāma gods among the deities of the Svāyambhuva Manvantara.
The sons of that Yajña were the Sabhāsvaras, born of Dakṣiṇā;
and from Prasūti, Dakṣa likewise begot twenty-four daughters. Listen to their names correctly from me: || 20 ||
Faith, Fortune, Fortitude, Contentment, Nourishment, Intelligence, Action, as well as Wisdom, Modesty, Body, Tranquility, Prosperity, and Fame as the thirteenth. || 21 ||
The lord Dharma accepted the daughters of Dakṣa as his wives.
From among them, eleven beautiful-eyed younger sisters remained.
Khyāti, Satī, then Sambhūti, Smṛti, Prīti, Kṣamā, as well as Sannati, Anasūyā, Ūrjā, Svāhā, and likewise Svadhā. || 23 ||
Bhṛgu, Bhava, and Marīci, as well as the sage Aṅgiras;
Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu, the best of ṛṣis. || 24 ||
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Vahni, and the Pitṛs—these best of sages received the daughters, Khyāti and the others, in due order. || 25 ||
Śraddhā gave birth to Kāma; Calā to Darpa; Dhṛti to Niyama, O son of Ātmaja;
Tuṣṭi to Saṃtoṣa; and Puṣṭi gave birth to Lobha. || 26 ||
Manu gave Ākūti to Ruci, Prasūti to Dakṣa,
and Devahūti to Kardama.
Medhā [gave birth to] Śruta; Kriyā [gave birth to] Daṇḍa, Naya, and Vinaya;
as well as Bodha and Buddhi; and Lajjā [gave birth to] Vinaya and Vapuḥ, her son. || 27 ||
Resolve was indeed born, and Peace gave birth to Tranquility; Prosperity gave birth to Happiness, and Glory to Fame—these are the sons of Dharma. || 28 ||
From Kāma were born Nandī and Harṣa, who begot Dharmapautra.
Himsā, however, was the wife of Adharma; from her was born Anṛta.
Kanyā is Nikṛti; from these two comes fear and indeed hell. Māyā and Vedanā likewise form this couple of theirs. || 30 ||
Then from those two was born Māyā, who brings about death and carries away all beings;
and Vedanā likewise gave birth to her own son, Duḥkha, from Raurava. || 31 ||
Death, disease, old age, sorrow, thirst, and anger were born;
for all these are known to be characterized by suffering and marked by unrighteousness. || 32 ||
They have neither wives nor sons, for they are all perpetual celibates (ūrdhvaretas).
O son of the best of sages, these forms of Viṣṇu are fierce;
indeed, they constantly bring about the dissolution of this world. || 33 ||

Then, O best of the twice-born, as he was crying out melodiously and running about,

The Sun, Water, Earth, Fire, Wind, and Space, as well as the initiated Brāhmaṇa and Soma—these are his bodies in successive order. || 8 ||
Likewise Suvarcalā, Omā, Vikeśī, and another Śivā; Svāhā, Dīśā, Dīkṣā, and Rohiṇī, in due order. || 9 ||

O best of men, the highly fortunate wives of Sūrya and the others are recorded along with their names, such as Rudrā and so forth; now hear from me about their offspring, by whose births and descendants this entire world is filled. || 10 ||
Śanaiścara, Śukra, Lohitāṅga, Manojava, Skanda, Svarga, Saṃtāna, and Budha were his sons in due order. || 11 ||
Rudra, being of such a nature, abandoned his wife Satī; and due to her anger toward Dakṣa, Satī cast off her own body. || 12 ||
O best of the twice-born, she became the daughter of Himavat by Menā;
her brother was Maināka, the peerless friend of the ocean. Then the blessed Lord Bhava married Umā once again, who was devoted to no other. || 13 ||
Khyāti gave birth to two gods, Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, from Bhṛgu, as well as Śrī, who is the consort of Nārāyaṇa, the God of gods. || 14 ||
**Chapter 9: Section One: Primary Creation and Secondary Emanation** Maitreya said:
"O Great Sage, you have related to me everything about which I questioned you."
"Tell me again this account of creation, beginning from the lineage of Bhṛgu! || 1.1 ||
Parāśara said: Lakṣmī, the consort of Viṣṇu, was born to Bhṛgu by Khyāti;
likewise, Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ were born as the two sons of Bhṛgu by Khyāti. 1.2.
Āyati and Niyati were the two daughters of the high-souled Meru;
they became the wives of Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, and from them both sons were born. || 1 ||
Prāṇa and my father Mṛkaṇḍu, who is of great renown, were born from him;
and I was born from him through Manasvinī.
Vedaśiras is my son.
He was born in Dhūmravatī;
now learn from me concerning Prāṇa as well!
The son of Prāṇa was Dyutimat.
And a son was born to him. || 2.1 ||
They had many sons and grandsons who were free from old age.
Marīci’s wife, Sambhūti, gave birth to Paurṇamāsa.
Viraja and Parvata were the two sons of that high-souled one;
O twice-born, I shall protect their sons in the recitation of the lineage.
Now hear also of the son of Prāṇa! || 2 ||
From Prāṇa was born his son Dyutimān, and from him came Rājavat; from him, O illustrious one, the lineage [proceeded].
Bhārgava has reached great renown.
O twice-born one, I shall now recount the sons of these two in the narration of their lineage. || 4 ||
And from Smṛti were born the sons of Aṅgiras, as well as daughters:
Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, and Anumati. || 5 ||
In that same manner, Anasūyā bore to Atri sons free from all blemish:
Soma, Durvāsas, and the yogi Dattātreya.
Dattoli was born as the son of Pulastya by his wife Prīti;
in a previous birth, during the Svārociṣa Manvantara, he is remembered as Agastya.
Kardama, Avarīyas, and Sahiṣṇu—these were the three sons whom Kṣamā, the wife of the progenitor Pulaha, gave birth to. || 8 ||
And Samnatī, the wife of Kratu, gave birth to the Bālakhilyas—sixty thousand ascetics whose vital energy was drawn upward. || 9 ||
To Urjā were born seven sons, each the size of a thumb-joint and possessing the brilliance of the blazing sun; these were indeed the sons of Vasiṣṭha.
Rajogātra, Ūrdhvabāhu, Savana, Anagha, Sutapas, and Śukra—these are all remembered as the seven ṛṣis. || 11 ||
From that Agni, who was the presiding deity and the first-born son of Brahmā,
the twice-born one obtained three sons of noble vigor by means of the Svāhā mantra.
Pāvaka, Pavamāna, Śuci, and also Jalāśin—there were forty-five others born in their lineage. || 13 ||
Thus, forty-nine fires have been proclaimed;
and these fires are further described as being that which consists of the father and his three sons. || 14 ||
The Pitṛs who were created by Brahmā and described by me to you— namely,
the Agniṣvāttas and the Barhiṣadas, those who are without fire and those who possess fire— || 15 ||
From them, Svadhā gave birth to Sūtā and likewise to Menā and Dhāriṇī.
O twice-born one, both of them were expounders of the Veda and both were practitioners of yoga. || 16 ||
Endowed with supreme knowledge and possessed of all virtues;
thus has this lineage of offspring of Dakṣa’s daughters been told.
One who remembers this with faith shall never be childless. || 16.1 ||
